speakers: Patrick Welton (founder and CEO, Welton Investment Corporation; trend following and managed futures manager, ex-Commodities Corporation)
summary: Podcast with Pat Welton, a 40-year trend follower and systematic macro manager. He argues trend returns decompose into economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion and reflexivity, and that volatility targeting, the four S's (setup, signal, sizing, symmetry) and client-goal alignment are the keys. He sees little capacity or multistrategy threat, flags zero rates and narrow G7 spreads as the real risk, and says investors' performance-chasing (return gap) is their biggest cost.

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: we were allocated more money every quarter as we hit return targets
claims.claim: Commodities Corporation, an early multistrategy pod shop, scaled each trader's capital in steps as return targets were hit, a performance-gated allocation scheme.
claims.direction: more capital to traders hitting return targets
claims.testable: partly - rule is described but no results given

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: when you start trading size, you can't only think about getting out when you want. you have to get out when the market lets you.
claims.claim: Once position size is large, exit timing is set by market liquidity rather than by the trader's wish, so size must be limited to what the market can absorb.
claims.direction: limit size to what liquidity allows
claims.conditions: large size relative to market depth
claims.testable: partly - testable via slippage versus size

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: markets weren't math. That there's somebody on the other side of every single trade who at that moment believes they also have an edge.
claims.claim: Every trade has a counterparty who believes they have an edge, so market structure and who is on the other side matter and returns are not pure mathematics.
claims.testable: no - philosophical framing

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the minute you take in outside money, you really take in the moral obligation that it's their goals that are most important for what you do with that money, which shapes everything.
claims.claim: Once a manager takes outside capital, the client's goals (not the manager's own) must drive risk and program design, which changes how risk is managed.
claims.testable: no - principle, not a rule

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: if they're more like an allocator than an investor, they might want something that is more consistently exposed and more constant and targeted volatility
claims.claim: Allocators who combine managers want constant, volatility-targeted exposure, whereas investors want exposure scaled up when forward return is better and down when it is weaker.
claims.direction: constant target volatility vs return-proportional sizing
claims.testable: partly - the two sizing rules can be backtested

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: So they think in dollars more than they think in percents.
claims.claim: Prop traders optimize risk-adjusted return on capital in dollar terms, which differs from an outside investor's percentage-return and risk goals.
claims.indicator: RAROC (risk-adjusted rate of return on capital)
claims.testable: no - descriptive

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: its average volatility would be in in well approximately probably about a 15v in the '9s but that might be 10 v when there's less opportunity and 20 when there's more
claims.claim: Welton's early trend program let volatility float, averaging about 15% in the 1990s, about 10% when opportunity was thin and about 20% when it was rich, rather than targeting a fixed level.
claims.direction: scale risk up when opportunity set is richer
claims.testable: yes - variable vs fixed vol target can be backtested

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: money three or four times faster than I make money.
claims.claim: Allocators found that some managers lost money three to four times faster than they made it, because positions expanded as volatility and correlation rose and reversals then hit a larger net exposure.
claims.indicator: loss speed vs gain speed ratio of P&L
claims.testable: yes - asymmetry of P&L speed is measurable in track records

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: when there was rising volatility which oftentimes accompanied by rising correlation that the overall net exposure was rising
claims.claim: Rising volatility often comes with rising correlation, so without risk scaling net portfolio exposure rises just before reversals, producing fast losses.
claims.testable: yes - compute net exposure vs correlation in a backtest

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: many people including ourselves began volatility targeting the portfolio or volatility targeting segments of the portfolio
claims.claim: In the early 2000s managers began volatility targeting the whole portfolio or segments of it to mute the fast-loss pattern and suit professional allocators.
claims.testable: yes - vol targeting vs none is a standard backtest

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: double the size of their account. I was almost certain that that was the end of any industry draw down.
claims.claim: Investor flows behave contrarian-to-timing: clients doubling an account tended to coincide with the end of an industry drawdown and clients halving it with the end of the good run.
claims.testable: partly - needs industry flow data

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: one of the most pernitious and damaging things I think traders have done to themselves is to respond to marketing feedback in the hopes of growing their business.
claims.claim: Changing a strategy in response to marketing feedback erodes the original edge and makes results worse over time.
claims.testable: partly - hard to test directly

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: How and where are you going to exploit that edge?
claims.claim: Decades ago a trader's interview came down to four questions: edge, where to exploit it, risk management or sizing, and how tails are protected.
claims.testable: no - checklist, not a testable rule

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: a pure trend follower has a very specific edge from agnosticism
claims.claim: A trend follower's edge comes from being agnostic and participating in many asset classes and in both directions, so the setup, signal, sizing and positive asymmetry all rely on multi-asset, multidirectional trading.
claims.direction: long and short across asset classes
claims.testable: yes - restrict markets or direction and compare

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: You are picking up return as that capital moves over months and quarters. It brings the convexity that is so valuable.
claims.claim: Trend followers earn return as capital moves between asset classes over months and quarters, which gives valuable convexity and skew at quarterly to semiannual horizons.
claims.testable: yes - measure skew and convexity of trend returns by horizon

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it's an incredibly useful property to have in in in a in a traditional portfolio.
claims.claim: Even though pure trend following has a return shape few investors like, its properties are very useful alongside a traditional stock-bond portfolio.
claims.indicator: trend following in a traditional portfolio
claims.testable: yes - portfolio blend backtest

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: Normally, the 4 S's would need to be satisfied.
claims.claim: A systematic approach should define four things: setup (the condition that raises probability), signal (entry and exit), sizing and symmetry (asymmetric payoff), and understanding each helps the trader stay with it.
claims.testable: partly - each S can be specified and tested, the framework itself is a checklist

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: sizing now includes forward opportunity and risk.
claims.claim: Position sizing should include forward-looking opportunity as well as risk, not just current volatility.
claims.direction: size up when forward opportunity is higher
claims.testable: yes - compare risk-only vs opportunity-adjusted sizing

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: have you entered a trade either directly or synthetically where you have an asymmetric advantage?
claims.claim: The symmetry question asks whether a trade has an asymmetric win/loss profile, either directly or synthetically, rather than an equal win to loss balance.
claims.testable: yes - payoff skew can be measured

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the difference between our success and other people's is that we actually follow our system
claims.claim: Success depends on following one's own system through rough and calm periods, which requires real confidence in it; even a published system fails in other hands.
claims.testable: partly - hard to measure

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: It's not much of a different step to then say the P&L of another trader is now just a price signal that then is used to replicate
claims.claim: Replicating managers by regressing on their P&L is the same logic as a trend follower using smoothed price as a signal, namely a reflection of others' actions.
claims.testable: yes - replication regressions can be run

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: reduced minimal market set sizes that replicate say the trend following industry
claims.claim: A reduced set of markets can replicate the trend following industry's returns, and popular trend ETFs would not have changed much if they had kept their market sets.
claims.indicator: minimal market set for trend replication
claims.testable: yes - Welton ran the work, results not given

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: if we do replicate the replicators we actually end up with better performance
claims.claim: Replicating the replicators gives better performance than the products because of a better smoothing coefficient, less churn and lower fees and cash management if fully funded.
claims.testable: yes - compare replica vs product net of costs

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: with the true statement that trends are behavioral
claims.claim: Trends are behavioral, but so are non-trending periods and high- and low-liquidity periods, since markets are the sum of participant behaviors.
claims.testable: no - narrative framing

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: one can decompose returns into the components of economic trend into financial carry into information diffusion and then into some form of reflexivity
claims.claim: Trend returns decompose into four sources: economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion and reflexivity (feedback loops), whose strength and time frame differ by sector.
claims.indicator: economic carry, financial carry, information diffusion, reflexivity
claims.direction: long positions held through time in trending markets
claims.conditions: strength varies by sector and time frame
claims.testable: yes - attribute trend returns to carry, trend and diffusion proxies

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: holding positions through time with one more feature some form of buying strength and selling weakness
claims.claim: Trend following is defined as holding positions through time while buying strength and selling weakness, not predicting; it can be long or short.
claims.testable: yes - definitional rule

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: have a positive positive economic carry, for instance, in equity indices, which is extremely strong, but have faced for most of the time a negative financial carry
claims.claim: Equity indices have strong positive economic carry but mostly negative financial carry, yet trend following still profits there.
claims.indicator: economic carry vs financial carry in equity indices
claims.testable: yes - carry measures can be computed

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: one will find that the majority and in some cases the vast majority of returns will be accumulated term structure premia.
claims.claim: In fixed income, trend returns come mostly from accumulated term structure (roll) premia, with little economic carry but strong financial carry.
claims.indicator: term structure premium (roll-down) in bond futures
claims.direction: long bond futures during carry-positive trends
claims.testable: yes - split trend return into carry and price

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: trend followers made 20 or 30% and almost everybody else missed on their predictions
claims.claim: In 2014 almost everyone forecast higher rates, yet rates fell all year and trend followers made 20 to 30%, showing the agnostic edge of following price instead of forecasts.
claims.direction: long bonds when rates trended down
claims.testable: yes - check 2014 trend returns

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: showing the return attributions plainly that they could even derive on their own
claims.claim: Showing investors a plain attribution of trend returns into carry, diffusion and reflexivity explains its zero correlation and positive convexity and persuades them.
claims.testable: partly - persuasion effect not testable

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: If I'm swimming for 20 hours, if I'm swimming for 3 seconds, the carry doesn't matter very much.
claims.claim: Carry matters only for long holding periods; short-term trading takes carry out of the equation and relies on information diffusion and reflexivity.
claims.testable: yes - carry contribution by holding period

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the impact of flows accelerating flows periodic flows rebalancing flows
claims.claim: Flows (accelerating, periodic and rebalancing flows) are far more useful drivers for holding periods under 10 days than classic trend signals.
claims.testable: yes - flow-based signals can be backtested

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: There's just a very narrow window when by the time you buy strength and sell weakness what's left in the middle is your potential profit.
claims.claim: Traditional trend following rarely works for 3 to 5 day holds because little profit remains between a buy-strength entry and a sell-weakness exit; academic short-term trend uses holds near a month.
claims.testable: yes - trend returns vs holding period

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: The macro trading uses only cross asset signals, fundamental signals, government reports, alternative data.
claims.claim: Welton's systematic macro book uses only cross-asset, fundamental, government report and alternative data signals, fully separate from price-based trend, giving diversification.
claims.indicator: cross-asset signals, government reports, alternative data
claims.testable: yes - separate macro sleeve can be built and tested

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the short-term models are all principally focused on flows with holding periods far less than 10 days typically
claims.claim: Welton's short-term models focus on flows with holding periods typically well under 10 days.
claims.testable: yes - flow signals

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: you can build say a dollarneutral currency basket now you're not stacking on top of your dollar risk
claims.claim: Relative value baskets neutralized for dollar risk, rate duration (DV01) or broad commodity exposure add diversification without stacking on the main portfolio's thematic risks.
claims.indicator: dollar-neutral FX basket, DV01-neutral rate basket, commodity-neutral basket
claims.testable: yes - build neutralized baskets and measure correlation to main book

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: a dedicated risk off sleeve which is only designed to sell equities when there's a rapid rise in flow data that shows us to have hedging and mispricing activities.
claims.claim: A dedicated risk-off sleeve sells equities when flow data show a rapid rise in hedging demand, because the manager earns an edge when others pay to neutralize risk.
claims.direction: sell equities on a rapid rise in hedging flows
claims.testable: yes - given a hedging-flow series

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: are massively underallocated to alternatives not over.
claims.claim: Of roughly $100 trillion of allocatable capital, investors are under-allocated to alternatives rather than over, which is bullish for multistrategy and managed futures demand.
claims.testable: no - opinion without data given

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the majority of hedge or of trend following returns are have been driven by accumulated economic and financial carries and information diffusion over months if not semianual
claims.claim: Trend returns come mostly from accumulated economic and financial carry and information diffusion over months to years, so multistrategy funds and short-term arbitrage are not what drives trend followers.
claims.indicator: economic and financial carry, information diffusion
claims.testable: yes - horizon decomposition of trend returns

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: It's definitely affected when spreads from in G7 environments all become extremely narrow and there's virtually no difference.
claims.claim: Trend following is hurt by zero-rate environments and by narrow spreads across G7 markets, because the carry components vanish, not by multistrategy trading.
claims.indicator: interest rate spreads across G7, zero rate level
claims.testable: yes - trend returns vs rate level and spread dispersion

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: if anything for most trend followers it's either not seen or it may even be providing a liquidity pool.
claims.claim: Short-term arbitrage and market-making trade the concave parts of markets, which trend followers either do not see or even supply liquidity to.
claims.testable: partly - hard to measure

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: trend following becomes this invaluable tool if they use it right.
claims.claim: Allocators who care about adverse multi-quarter moves, such as pensions facing a two-sigma liability shock, need better tail coverage, and trend following gives it if sized properly (portable alpha, volatility level).
claims.direction: allocate to trend for tail coverage
claims.conditions: depends on allocation size, opportunity cost, vol
claims.testable: yes - portfolio stress tests

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: This whole narrative that a trend follower can get too big and somehow their returns will go away.
claims.claim: A trend follower owning 200 of the 250 billion in industry capacity with the same approach would see the same performance, since size alone does not remove returns if methods are diversified.
claims.testable: partly - thought experiment, not empirical

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: You would be the industry.
claims.claim: If one firm ran hundreds of different systematic approaches it would lose its edge and just match the industry average.
claims.testable: no - qualitative

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: those kinds of changes practically need to take place over years for client acceptance
claims.claim: Managers that need to diversify methods to absorb more assets face style-drift pushback, so changes must take years, which makes fast asset raising a capacity risk.
claims.testable: no - business dynamic

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: people are very diligent about seeing the fingerprint of their execution costs and their execution alpha and they begin to see their execution costs rise objectively measured
claims.claim: A manager can detect a capacity problem when objectively measured execution costs trend upward, usually first in a few markets before all.
claims.indicator: execution cost and execution alpha tracking
claims.testable: yes - track slippage per market over time

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: a large volume of dollars trying to go in a into a smaller market more rapidly is going to press a market
claims.claim: Slippage rises with dollar volume relative to market size and speed of trading; small money in a large market, trading slowly, does not move prices.
claims.indicator: market impact vs order size and speed
claims.conditions: size relative to liquidity; liquidity varies by time of day
claims.testable: yes - impact models

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: you could trade that much in copper but you can't trade that much in tin
claims.claim: Capacity differs by market, so a large program must size each commodity to its depth (copper versus tin).
claims.testable: yes - cap position by volume

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: and six months later it will return to its liquidity.
claims.claim: A rise in execution costs in one market can be temporary, with liquidity returning within months, or permanent because there is too much money there, so it needs diagnosis.
claims.testable: yes - persistence of cost changes

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: If you have one that if you delay by 15 minutes, you lose 20% of your P&L, you have one that's pretty time-sensitive.
claims.claim: Strategies with long holding periods that are insensitive to a one-day execution delay have more capacity and a larger margin of error than strategies that lose a fifth of P&L from a 15-minute delay.
claims.testable: yes - delay test in backtest

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: objectivity the man the the emotional manifestation of that is is humility
claims.claim: Objectivity, expressed as humility, is the key to trading and drives ongoing research as markets and microstructure change.
claims.testable: no - disposition

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: are rates rising rates falling, inflation up, inflation down.
claims.claim: Regimes are best viewed as macro biases, rates rising or falling and inflation up or down; they help but also mislead early quants.
claims.testable: yes - regime classification

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: this this sort of two-body problem
claims.claim: Early quants model data changes as moving the market in a two-body problem and cannot explain why the same data surprise sometimes causes big moves and sometimes none.
claims.testable: yes - market response to surprises varies by regime

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: data changes and surprises don't buy or sell anything. People see those signals.
claims.claim: Data surprises do not move prices; people do, so which data matters shifts over time, as when M1-M3 money supply once led the Wall Street Journal and is now ignored.
claims.indicator: money supply M1-M3, economic data surprises
claims.testable: yes - market sensitivity by data series over time

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: Um, you might want to trade differently in a high inflation, you know, rising interest rate, supply constrained world than you might want to do in a demand constrained, low interest rate, low inflation world.
claims.claim: Trading approach should differ between high-inflation, rising-rate, supply-constrained regimes and demand-constrained, low-rate, low-inflation regimes; regime shifting is an imperfect setup, not a precise prediction.
claims.testable: yes - regime-conditional backtests

claims.speaker: Patrick Welton
claims.quote: the return gap the negative investor alpha that occurs from people switching on performance is is usually the biggest cost that they face
claims.claim: Investors who switch managers based on performance suffer a negative return gap, usually their biggest cost; steady-handedness compounds best.
claims.indicator: investor return gap vs fund return
claims.testable: yes - dollar-weighted vs time-weighted return
